passages.title: Tallest tree species - Guinness World Records
passages.text: Tallest tree species - Who Redwood, Douglas fir, Eucalyptus - What 113 metre(s) - Where Not Applicable - When 2012 Redwoods (genera Sequoia and Sequoiadendron), eucalypts (genus Eucalyptus, often called gum trees) and the Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), a type of pine, share the distinction of being the world’s tallest tree species. All types of tree have been recorded growing to heights of over 113 metres (372 feet). Currently, only six tree species have living individuals taller than 95 m (311 ft 8 in): four are from the west coast of North America (Sequoia sempervirens, Pseudotsuga menziesii, Picea sitchensis and Sequoiadendron giganteum); one is from south-east Australia (Eucalyptus regnans); and one is from Malaysian Borneo (Shorea faguetiana).

Yellow Meranti (Richetia faguetiana) A yellow meranti is the tallest tropical tree in the world and the third-tallest tree overall. Menara, the tallest meranti, is located in the Malaysian State of Sabah on the island of Borneo. It stands 330 feet (100 meters) tall. In 2019, a field researcher with the South East Asia Rainforest Research Partnership verified this height by climbing the tree and releasing a tape measure. Before this, height records were tied to a Sabah grove found in 2016, where the meranti measured above 295 feet (90 meters). The yellow meranti is a tall tropical hardwood that produces yellow flowers. The tree species is native to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines, though its wild populations are at risk. passages.text: Cypress (Cupressus torulosa) The tallest tree in Asia grows in the deepest canyon in the world. Situated in southeastern Tibet, the Yarlung Zangbo Grand Canyon reaches a maximum depth of over 19,714 feet (6,009 meters). In 2023, researchers from Beijing's Peking University discovered an unrecorded Himalayan cypress growing inside it. The cypress turned out to be the second-tallest recorded tree in the world, measuring 335 feet (102 meters) tall. The Himalayan cypress is an evergreen conifer native to the western Himalayas. Although these trees typically only grow up to 150 feet (46 meters) tall, outliers can grow much higher. The cypress found in Yarlung Zangbo was not alone in its height. Using lasers, drones, and radar tools, researchers found several other towering trees in the area, standing over 279 feet (85 meters) tall. Wild Himalayan cypresses are rare in China, making them a first-class protected plant species. Although the tallest is located in the Yarlung Zangbo Grand Canyon National Nature Reserve, it is not accessible to tourists due to the harsh landscape. passages.text: The Tallest Trees In The World The world's list of tallest trees is constantly changing. With modern technology letting us explore spaces we couldn't before, researchers are still finding and measuring new forest giants. In 2006, the title of world's tallest tree changed when a new coast redwood was discovered. The tallest tree in Asia was also discovered in 2023, replacing the former record holder. As of 2026, these are the tallest trees in the world that we know of. However, it's possible that even taller titans are hidden in unexplored pockets of the world. Coast Redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) Coast redwoods are the tallest trees in the world by a fairly large margin. Naturalists found Hyperion, the tallest known redwood, in a quiet part of California's Redwood National Park in 2006. American forest ecologist Dr. Stephen Sillett measured the redwood's height at 379 feet (115 meters). Before this, the Stratosphere Giant coast redwood was thought to be the highest tree in the world, at 370 feet (112 meters) tall. As of 2026, Hyperion remains the tallest tree we know of. passages.text: Sitka spruce is Canada's tallest known tree. The 315-foot (96-meter) Carmanah Giant can be found in Carmanah Walbran Provincial Park on Vancouver Island. In California, some of the world's tallest Sitka spruces grow amongst redwoods. In addition to the record-breaker in Redwood National Park, a 276-foot (84-meter) giant grows in Prairie Creek Redwoods State Park. Douglas-Fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) The world's tallest Douglas-fir was dethroned in 2025. Previously, the Doerner Fir in Southern Oregon measured highest in its species, at 327 feet (100 meters). However, a 2025 wildfire caused the 450-year-old tree to lose about 50 feet of height, shifting the record. Previously second-tallest, the Douglas-fir that took its place measures 326 feet (99 meters) high. The unnamed tree was found and measured in Redwood National and State Parks in 2022. Native to North America, Douglas-firs are split into two varieties. The Rocky Mountain variety lives in the interior west. It grows up to 160 feet (49 meters) tall and rarely lives longer than 400 years. The world's current tallest Douglas-fir is part of the coast variety. Although the tallest known Sitka spruce was found in Redwood National Park, other massive trees grow in Washington and British Columbia. Its bark and needles are also resistant to salt spray. Sitka spruce populations are generally stable across their natural range.
